title: The Founding Fathers Show
format: talk show on a sofa: host plus four recurring guests, one era per episode, 45 to 60 minutes, four segments (the greeting, the catch-up, the reaction, the closing question)

fiction.disclosure: The likeness is deliberate and openly absurd: illustrated caricature, one permanent chyron reading not a real interview, and the host says on camera that these are actors in a comedy about history. Nothing here is presented as authentic footage.

guardrails: illustrated or animated likeness only, never photoreal synthetic video of a real historical figure that could be mistaken for archival footage
no invented quotation is ever presented as authentic: a founder's position is grounded in his own writings with the source named, and where the host is extrapolating he says so in the line before
every historical claim carries a source in the episode's show notes
tragedies are explained, never mocked: the comedy is the guests' incomprehension of a century they missed, and the host states plainly what happened and to whom
no modern partisan framing put in a founder's mouth as though his own writings support it; where a modern analogy is made, it is named as the host's analogy
the guests stay dead: no episode pretends they have opinions on a living person's conduct beyond what the format's satire explicitly frames

episode_zero.title: The War to End All Wars, Explained to Men Who Started One
beats: the greeting: they arrive mid-argument from 1787, and the host has to explain what a camera is before anything else
the catch-up: 1914 to 1918 in nine minutes, archival stills, a map that fills in as the front moves
the reaction: each guest answers from his own writings, the host names the source, and at least one answer is a guess labelled as one
the disagreement: two of them take incompatible lessons from it, and nobody is corrected for the sake of the audience
the closing question: what would you have done in 1917, answered in character, then the chyron and the outro
